http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-distribution

What do others think? I don't just want to add everything and
the kitchen sink to Stan as a function. It'll be confusing to use
and hard to maintain. But any distribution that's at all widely
used should be fair game.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: modified Bessel functions
parts:
On Thursday, May 30, 2013 6:30:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
What do others think?  I don't just want to add everything and
the kitchen sink to Stan as a function.  It'll be confusing to use
and hard to maintain.  But any distribution that's at all widely
used should be fair game.

Speaking more philosophically rather than about the K-distribution specifically, I would say that Stan should make some effort to include unpopular distributions. Some distributions are unpopular largely because they do not lend themselves to maximum likelihood or Gibbs sampling but are otherwise plausible distributions for likelihoods or priors. Maybe the K-distribution is an example. Similarly, many distributions have "generalized" variants with additional parameters that aren't used that much because people don't want to specify particular fixed values for them but don't want to optimize over them either (e.g. the exponent in scobit models). Stan could add a lot of value in these situations by making it easy to utilize some unpopular distribution.

Of course, there are an infinite number of distributions and the manual would eventually look like Johnson, Kotz, and Balakrishnan. But I think we should be trying to drive demand a little rather than simply saying we'll try to implement distributions that are in demand.

Ben

On Thursday, May 30, 2013 7:41:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Of course, there are an infinite number of distributions and the manual would eventually look like Johnson, Kotz, and
> Balakrishnan.

I don't know that book, but in looking it up, the chapters
seem to only scratch the surface of what's on Wikipedia.

That book (actually books; they came in two volumes) was Wikipedia for statistical distributions before there was Wikipedia. Of course, Wikipedia seems to only scratch the surface of what's on

http://blog.wolfram.com/2013/02/01/the-ultimate-univariate-probability-distribution-explorer/

Anyway, it seems to me that good Stan usage would typically involve the 3, 4, 5, .... parameter likelihoods, unless there was strong reason to use a 2 parameter distribution. It is not as if anyone really knows what distribution is correct, but you have a better chance with a less restrictive distribution. And it is basically just as easy to use a 3, 4, 5, ... parameter likelihood --- iff said distribution is implemented in Stan --- as it is to use the 2 parameter distribution; you just have to put some reasonable prior on the extra parameter(s). So pushing Stan in this direction would encourage better statistical practice. Like you said, I think LKJ was a step in this direction.

Ben

Anyway, it seems to me that good Stan usage would typically involve the 3, 4, 5, .... parameter likelihoods, unless there was strong reason to use a 2 parameter distribution. It is not as if anyone really knows what distribution is correct, but you have a better chance with a less restrictive distribution. And it is basically just as easy to use a 3, 4, 5, ... parameter likelihood --- iff said distribution is implemented in Stan --- as it is to use the 2 parameter distribution; you just have to put some reasonable prior on the extra parameter(s). So pushing Stan in this direction would encourage better statistical practice. Like you said, I think LKJ was a step in this direction.

Maybe I should rephrase myself. I don't think we should try to implement every distribution that is (approximately) a special case of some other distribution. But we should try to eventually implement almost every distribution that is not a special case of anything else. And if some user really wants some distribution that is special case, they can impose some restrictions on the parameters of a more general distribution (and maybe Stan could facilitate that).

In other words, if we didn't already have the gamma distribution, I wouldn't think it would be a priority to implement it when we could spend our effort implementing the generalized gamma distribution. I was going to link to the generalized gamma distribution on Wikipedia, except Wikipedia told me that the generalized gamma is just a special case of something called the Amoroso distribution, which I had never heard of. But this paper

http://threeplusone.com/Crooks-Amoroso.pdf

says it is a special case of both the generalized beta and generalized beta prime distributions. Ergo, Stan needs to implement the generalized beta

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_beta_distribution

Ben

The generalized beta doesn't look that difficult to
implement. It would then be tempting to say we have all
of these:

http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/62/GBtree.jpg

But one issue is that some of these require parameters tending
toward infinity. So we might have to code it with special conditions
inside recognizing floating point infinity.

Even if we did that, I see two reasons to implement simpler distributions.

1. It's less confusing to users, who may not want to
configure the generalized beta distribution to get a gamma
and then configure that to get an exponential.

2. They're more efficient.

We could work on 2 directly in Stan. For 1, we could supply prepackages
configs, but that's essentially just doing the simpler distributions
if we also make them more efficient.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: very generally parameterized distributions
parts:
On Friday, May 31, 2013 12:15:07 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
But one issue is that some of these require parameters tending
toward infinity.  So we might have to code it with special conditions
inside recognizing floating point infinity.

Yeah, that is an issue. But, a lot of times a number that is "only" in the hundreds or thousands is tantamount to infinity in terms of affecting the shape of the distribution. We still might have some trouble with that until RMHMC lands. Another thing is that sometimes you can parameterize it in terms of the reciprocal of that diverging thing so that you get special cases as the parameter approaches 0 from above.

Even if we did that, I see two reasons to implement simpler distributions.

1.  It's less confusing to users, who may not want to
configure the generalized beta distribution to get a gamma
and then configure that to get an exponential.

2.  They're more efficient.

We could work on 2 directly in Stan.  For 1, we could supply prepackages
configs, but that's essentially just doing the simpler distributions
if we also make them more efficient.

If we, for example, had the generalized beta, then it is not that much additional work to add (possibly less efficient) special cases where the body of the function just inlines a call to the generalized beta. And maybe we tweak the generalized beta to handle some special cases more efficiently. Even with all that, maybe it becomes worthwhile to have a completely separate function with an optimized implementation, but someone can do those as necessary.

But the main point is that we can kill a lot of birds with one stone if that stone is among the relatively few known 5 parameter distributions.

Ben
